problem: If ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066703/assets/32e9cba3d7ee75019489dcc8a9c82f1b854bfa77af49e22fa9f51d4412cba95d.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066703/assets/dc64b0c557c838cf31e652ebdb8eee91d1fee8c947b343b16fceaf765c1f8517.png) are solutions to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ find $A\mathbf{w}(t)$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14066703/assets/64b157c381c05102b51320592e61ffff5c4d611af4bd15679f1f2b38f3d01b10.png)
worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{u}(t)$ and $\mathbf{v}(t)$ are solutions to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ the superposition principle guarantees that 

$$
c\mathbf{u}(t) + d\mathbf{v}(t)
$$

 is also a solution to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)$ for all $c,d\in\mathbb{R}.$

Notice that 

$$
\mathbf{w}(t)=4\mathbf{u}(t)+6\mathbf{v}(t).
$$

 

Therefore, $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t).$ So, in order to find $A\mathbf{w}(t)$ we just need to find $\mathbf{w}'(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Aw & ={w}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(4{e}^{4t})^{′} \\ (6{e}^{5t})^{′}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16{e}^{4t} \\ 30{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
